summary: The note lists ten destinations where school field trips and ecotourism are used to teach environmental education after September 1, 2023. Each entry names a site and a teacher or guide who led a trip, along with the ecological topics students studied. The note concludes that firsthand experience of nature builds environmental stewardship and a more environmentally literate generation.
one_line: Ten field trip destinations, from Redwood to the Galápagos, that teach students environmental stewardship through hands-on experiences in nature.
key_facts: Matthew Greene, an environmental science teacher, took students to Redwood National and State Parks in California on Sept. 15, 2023, to study some of the world's tallest trees and old-growth forests.

Jenny Larson, a geography teacher, led an October 10 outing to Yellowstone National Park in Wyoming, where students observed geothermal features and wildlife and did water sampling and wildlife tracking.
Yellowstone is described as the first national park in the world.
Biology teacher David Thompson led a November 5 trip to the Everglades in Florida, stressing wetlands' role in water purification and as storm buffers.
Sarah Kim and other educators took history and science classes to the Grand Canyon in Arizona on September 25 to study desert ecosystems, water resources and Native American tribes.
Marine science teacher James Patterson took students to the Great Barrier Reef in Australia on December 3 to study coral reef ecosystems and climate change.

Students from Lincoln High School visited Costa Rica's Monteverde Cloud Forest Reserve on November 20, led by environmental educator Maria Rodriguez, focusing on tropical biology and sustainable living.
Robert Carter, an outdoor education expert, guided a Wilson Secondary student group in Banff National Park, Canada, on October 18, explaining glaciology and alpine ecosystems.
Naturalist Emily Stone led students to Glacier National Park in Montana on September 8, where retreating glaciers illustrated climate change.
Laura Bennett, a science department head, led a November 28 field trip to the Amazon Rainforest in Brazil, where students engaged with local conservation efforts and communities.
Biology teacher Mark Stevens took students to the Galápagos Islands in Ecuador on December 15 to study evolution, natural selection and endemic species.
The note concludes that field trips and ecotourism inspire students to become conscientious citizens and promise a more environmentally literate and responsible generation.
